a:r.a:t: GPCRs Can Use Other Secondary Messenger Molecules

p:cNvPr.descr: Diagram of how hormone-activated phospholipase C and IP3 are produced. Diagram of how hormone-activated phospholipase C and IP3 are produced. This diagram shows seven stages in the process, all of which occur in the cytoplasm, lined with small, light blue spheres that represent the plasma membrane. In stage 1, the hormone, indicated by a small circle marked H, binds to a specific receptor, which is shown as a pinkish structure with red and tan looped ribbons on the inside. The top of the receptor is in the extracellular space. Towards the bottom of the cytoplasm is a green, snail-like structure with two projections at the top, protruding into the cytoplasm. This green structure is labeled Gq alpha, and in it, there is a gray oval, labeled GDP. An arrow pointing away from the green structure starts off white and slowly turns to the same shade of green as the previously-described structure as it points to another green structure that only has one projection into the cytoplasm. The arrow has two smaller, curved arrows, one curved downward, illustrating the loss of GDP. The other arrow points into the larger green arrow and shows GTP entering. This is the second stage of the process, where the occupied receptor causes an GDP-GTP exchange on Gq alpha. The Gq alpha, which is represented by one green structure with one projection into the cytoplasm and has hair-like extensions all around it, is bound to GTP. In stage 3, the Gq alpha bound to GTP moves to phospholipase C (PLC), which is represented as a light blue bulb in the cytoplasm. Next to that is a red sphere that is mixed in with the plasma membrane; from it, two red projections labeled PIP2 can be seen. A long, curved arrow points downward from the small red sphere to a half of a small red sphere in another receptor embedded in the plasma membrane on the bottom of the diagram. In stages 4 and 5, active PLC cleaves PIP2 to IP3 and diacylglycerol. IP3 binds to a specific receptor-gated Ca2 channel, releasing a chose Ca2 plus, represented by small purple spheres. Another arrow points away from PIP2 to diacylglycerol, which is the same shape as PIP2, but has half of a red sphere instead of a whole one. In stages 6 and 7, an arrow points away from diacylglycerol to another diacylglycerol, which is connected to a protein kinase C receptor, represented by a light blue structure. The Ca2 plus that was released in stage 5 is inside of the protein kinase C receptor; a black arrow points away from this structure. Stage 7 reads, “Phosphorylation of cellular proteins by protein kinase C produces some of the cellular responses to the hormone.”
